 1 Task Description
 BDK provides solution to the problem of beam stability. It determines the stability eigenvalues for buckling of a straight individual member. The member, which is taken from the entire sys- tem, is calculated with STAR2 or ASE and the buckling resistance check of steel members is performed according to the specified design code.
 1.1 Task Outline
 At first, the user defines the system selecting straight, individual beam or truss elements, which are cut out of the entire structural system and are treated independently. The program allows the user to explicitly define the support conditions at the start and end of each selected indi- vidual beam, as well as continuous supports, offering a complete control on the properties of the selected system. Furthermore, standards-related design parameters may also be explicitly defined.
 Having available the complete system, the program sets up and solves the formed stability eigenvalue problem and the eigenvalues and eigenforms are determined for a pre-specified and calculated loadcase. Following the eigenvalues determination and taking into considera- tion the defined design parameters, BDK performs the buckling check according to the selected design code.
 1.2 Supported Design Codes
 The design checks are performed according to one of the following supported standards:
 • DIN 18800-2 / OEN 4300: Structural steelwork analysis of safety against buckling of linear members and frames [1].
 • EN 1993-1-1: Design of steel structures - Part 1-1: General rules and rules for buildings [2].
 • BS 5950-1: Structural use of steelwork in building [3].
 1.3 Assumptions and Limitations
 BDK can determine the stability eigenvalues under the following assumptions:
 • General, also unsymmetric cross-sections
 • General tapered sections (along the beam axis)
 • Straight beam axis and centric haunches
 • Change of the boundary conditions including the elastic warping constraint and distributed support.

1.3 Assumptions and Limitations. BDK can determine the stability eigenvalues under the following assumptions:. • General, also unsymmetric cross-sections. • General tapered sections (along the beam axis). • Straight beam axis and centric haunches. • Change of the boundary conditions including the elastic warping constraint and distributed support..
 • Solution for the complete lateral torsional buckling problem or for the plain lateral buckling problem with disregard of the normal force.
 For the calculation of the lateral torsional buckling safety for an individual beam, according to DIN 18800-2, the assumptions of this design code hold. This implies that the design is strictly valid only for double symmetric I and H sections, without the intended torsional loading.
 Materials, section profiles and the design code to comply with, are selected by the user at the early steps of defining the total structural system. Regardless of the initial design standard selection, the user may explicitly redefine in the BDK task the specification of a different design standard (see NORM). This practice should be done with caution, since significant differences exist between the design codes, regarding material mechanical behaviour and properties as well as the considered safety factors.
 Furthermore, a cross-section of class 4 of EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-5 can be treated, since the calculation of the effective cross-section values in BDK is available.
 Warning
 At the current version of BDK, it is possible to calculate only the effective properties for THIN-WALLED cross-sections (Iterative Method). Another approach would be to use the SIG NEFF input in AQUA, which works both for solid, as well as for thin-walled cross- sections. Please refer to the VERIFICATION Manual Design - Example DCE-EN 30.
 For the determination of the critical force and moment for buckling, always an eigenvalue anal- ysis is performed, except of explicitly user-defined buckling lengths. In the unlikely event that the eigenvalue analysis fails, analytical formulas are used.

A model system can consist of several beam or truss elements, forming a member, although there are no individual supports between its endings, other than the optionally defined. The user can select any straight beam or truss element to cut out of the entire structural system. Each selected member is then treated by BDK as an individual independent system, taking into account the inner forces and displacements derived from the parental system analysis for a considered loadcase. For a member that represents a subsystem of the total system, the corresponding support conditions have to be defined carefully. This applies in particular to the sway perpendicular to the system plane, for the case where the system was entered as a planar system.

The start and end boundary conditions can be defined using the CVA and CVE input. With- out this specification, they are set to Fork-Fork. Moreover, BDK assumes that there are no intermediate individual supports between the endings of the selected member, other than the optionally defined intermediate supports (CVM), lateral restraints (CVL), and continuous sup- ports (CV). Therefore, the user should explicitly enter the exact boundary conditions at both ends (CVA / CVE) and in between them (CVM / CVL / CV). For this purpose, different input options are available:
 the assignment of spring constant values,
 the definition of fixities using the literal FIX,
 •
 the automatic computation of the spring constant values using the literal AUTO.
 •
 The supports thus defined are oriented in the local directions of the member.
 In the case of the literal AUTO, the corresponding spring constant value of a support is auto- matically determined by a linear analysis of the global structure. This value is independent of the design load case. Hence, imperfections or second order effects are not incorporated. It should be also noted that the supports only constrain single degrees of freedom and do not couple them. Therefore, coupling effects are considered in a simplified way. Between different nodes, coupling effects are neglected. The literal AUTO can be used in the CVA, CVE, and CVM input.
 The automatic calculation of the boundary conditions (AUTO) supports parallel processing of the elements and uses a parallel finite element solver. This means, that the performance may be improved by using multicore processors.
 Hint
 See Example 58 of the VERIFICATION Manual Mechanical for a demonstration of the automatic computation of the spring constant values.

Literature and design codes distinguish between the following cases for beam structures:
 • Lateral Torsional Buckling: the most general case of buckling where deflections towards both axes as well as torsional rotation (twist) occur.
 • Lateral Buckling: lateral deflection and torsional rotation (twist).
 • Flexural Buckling: buckling about the strong or weak axis, in-plane deformation, no tor- sional rotation.
 • Torsional Buckling: buckling about the longitudinal axis, torsional rotation (twist), the beam axis remain straight.

The case of buckling will occur if an element will suffer from large forces due to small defor- mations induced by geometric non-linear effects. This will limit the ultimate load for slender structures.

As both theories are not applicable in a general case, their results will define basic design parameters used for the combined design of the effects.

sections: 2.7 Lateral torsional buckling according to EN 1993-1-1 [2]
2.7.1 Interaction factors - Annex A, Annex B

content:
For the determination of the interaction factors kyy, kyz, kzy, kzz, both methods of Annex A and B of EN 1993-1-1[2], have been implemented. The interaction factors have been derived from two alternative approaches. The National Annex may give a choice from alternative method 1 or alternative method 2. The application range of the two methods is in both cases basically a single span member of doubly symmetrical cross section subjected to axial compression, end-moments and transverse loading [8].
 Hint
 Both, method 1 (Annex A) and method 2 (Annex B) have been developed by ECCS. An essential difference in the application between these two methods is, that in the method 1 no possibility is provided to take into account the intermediate supports and lateral restraints for the LTB analysis. In method 2 the intermediate and lateral supports may be taken into account in the k,j interaction factors.
 • Annex A, Method 1: The intention of the formulae for Method 1 is to present general, transparent, consistent and accurate interaction criteria, as described in ECCS TC 8 - No. 119 [7]. Each factor involved in this formulae is linked with a physical effect, which allows for the influence of the different phenomena to be represented. This method can represent both members susceptible and not susceptible to torsional deformation.
 Various factors in this method, need to be determined explicitly. BDK employs the eigen- value analysis to determine them and does not derive them from analytical formulas, in order to offer a more accurate representation of the system under consideration:
 – ¯λ0, representing the reduced slenderness for lateral torsional buckling for the partic- ular case of constant bending moment,
 – C1, the factor depending on the bending moment distribution and end restraints con- ditions,
 – Ncr,T, the torsional critical force,
 – ¯λm, the maximum non-dimensional slenderness.

The analysis procedure for the lateral torsional buckling design is made according to DIN 18800, Part 2 Element 301, where it says: For the simplification of beams, continuous beams and frames, one can evaluate flexural buckling and lateral torsional buckling separately. Whereby the flexural buckling analysis is followed by the lateral torsional buckling analysis. Each analysis is made for individual beams, which are picked from the entire system. Each beam is subjected to the beam-end internal forces and moments, which are determined for the entire system.
 The flexural buckling analysis is made with the programs STAR2 or ASE. All the individual beams, of the system being analysed for flexural buckling, are provided with support conditions, usually torsional restraints are applied. The STAR2 or ASE calculation has to be made with ultimate loads or γ-factor loads. Whereby the analysis procedure elastic-elastic or plastic- plastic (non-linear theory) according to DIN 18800, Part 2 Table 101 is possible in STAR2 or ASE. All the elasto-plastic regions must be fixed laterally against torsion and deformation, which is required for the conservation of the cross-section.
 The individual checks are then calculated with the equations from the elements 310, 318 and 321 of the DIN 18800-2.

The table defines **CVA** input parameters used by a BDK system to specify **beam support stiffness characteristics** for subsequent **MEMB** element input. It references related concepts such as **CVE** and **MEMB**, and notes that, as a default, BDK employs a **fork support condition**. The support stiffness values are applied in the **local beam directions**. Each support component is characterized either as a **spring constant** (positive value) or a **fixity** (negative value). A value of **-1.0** or the literal **FIX** indicates a **fixed constraint**. The literal **AUTO** triggers automatic computation of the corresponding spring constant. Importantly, these CVA values are **active only for the subsequent MEMB input**.

The table columns are:

- **Item**: short code identifying the stiffness parameter.
- **Description**: meaning of the parameter and the physical effect it represents.
- **Unit**: engineering units for the parameter.
- **Default**: default value used if the parameter is not explicitly set.

### Parameter definitions and defaults

1. **CB** – *Spring constant warping bi-moment*  
   - **Unit:** kN/m³  
   - **Default:** 0  
   - Represents stiffness against warping bi-moment effects.

2. **CY** – *Spring constant for lateral displacement in local Y direction*  
   - **Unit:** kN/m  
   - **Default:** ∞ (infinite stiffness / effectively restrained)  
   - Governs lateral displacement behavior along Y.

3. **CZ** – *Spring constant for lateral displacement in local Z direction*  
   - **Unit:** kN/m  
   - **Default:** ∞  
   - Governs lateral displacement behavior along Z.

4. **DX** – *Rotational spring constant for torsion*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m/rad  
   - **Default:** ∞  
   - Models stiffness resisting torsional rotation.

5. **DY** – *Rotational spring constant for moment about Y*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m/rad  
   - **Default:** 0  
   - Represents rotational restraint associated with moment My.

6. **DZ** – *Rotational spring constant for moment about Z*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m/rad  
   - **Default:** 0  
   - Represents rotational restraint associated with moment Mz.

When retrieving, it’s essential to connect the codes (CB, CY, CZ, DX, DY, DZ) to: (a) their physical meaning (warping, lateral Y/Z, torsion, rotational moments Y/Z), (b) their units, and (c) their default boundary behavior (∞ meaning effectively fixed in that degree of freedom; 0 meaning no rotational restraint for DY/DZ and no warping stiffness for CB).

The input table defines spring-related stiffness parameters that are applied to a beam through the local beam support condition. These values are meant to be used as part of the **MEMB** input (i.e., they become effective only for the subsequent **MEMB** definition). The table provides six stiffness entries controlling warping, lateral translational springs, and rotational springs (including moments about specific rotational degrees of freedom).

### General meaning and sign conventions
For the underlying support mechanism (described in the surrounding context), supports are defined in the **local directions of the beam**. The stiffness values are expressed as **spring constants** using **positive values**. A value of **-1.0** (or the literal **FIX**) represents a **fixed constraint** rather than a spring with finite stiffness. The literal **AUTO** triggers an automatic computation of a spring constant. While that context discusses support definition, the parameters below specifically define the spring constants that characterize those supports.

### Table structure
Columns:
- **Item**: Identifier code for the parameter.
- **Description**: Human-readable meaning.
- **Unit**: Physical units for the stiffness.
- **Default**: Default value if not provided.

### Parameters
1. **CB** – *Spring constant for warping bi-moment*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m³  
   - **Default:** 0  
   - Interpretation: Controls the stiffness associated with **warping bi-moment** effects, typically relevant to advanced beam torsion/warping behavior.

2. **CY** – *Spring constant for lateral displacement y*  
   - **Unit:** kN/m  
   - **Default:** ∞ (infinity)  
   - Interpretation: Represents the translational spring stiffness resisting motion in the **local y direction**. An infinite value corresponds to an effectively restrained (very stiff) condition.

3. **CZ** – *Spring constant for lateral displacement z*  
   - **Unit:** kN/m  
   - **Default:** ∞  
   - Interpretation: Translational spring stiffness resisting motion in the **local z direction**.

4. **DX** – *Rotational spring constant Torsion*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m/rad  
   - **Default:** ∞  
   - Interpretation: Rotational stiffness associated with **torsional rotation** about the relevant axis.

5. **DY** – *Rotational spring constant Moment My*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m/rad  
   - **Default:** 0  
   - Interpretation: Rotational stiffness related to the **My moment** response (rotation corresponding to the local rotational degree associated with My). Default 0 means no rotational spring resistance for this moment contribution.

6. **DZ** – *Rotational spring constant Moment Mz*  
   - **Unit:** kN·m/rad  
   - **Default:** 0  
   - Interpretation: Rotational stiffness related to the **Mz moment** response. Default 0 means rotationally free with respect to that moment contribution.

### Practical effect
Together, these entries allow modeling of beam end/support compliance in translations (Y, Z) and rotations (torsion plus My and Mz), as well as optional coupling to warping behavior (CB). Default settings strongly constrain lateral translation and torsion (∞ for CY, CZ, DX) while leaving certain rotational moment stiffnesses free (0 for DY, DZ), and warping bi-moment stiffness inactive (CB = 0).

The table defines three input parameters used to specify **torsional and translational support stiffnesses** for a structural model. It is presented as a set of “Item” entries with an accompanying description, unit, and default value. These stiffness values are intended to be **manually provided by the user**, and they are described as inputs that become **active only for the subsequent MEMB input** (i.e., they apply to the next step/configuration rather than the current one).

### Items and meanings

1. **DX — Torsional support**  
   - **Description:** Represents the torsional stiffness provided by the support.  
   - **Unit:** `kNm/m/rad`  
   - **Default:** `0`  
   - **Interpretation:** This value is a rotational stiffness term expressed as torsional resistance per unit length and per radian (units indicate moment per length per radian of twist). If left at the default, torsional support is effectively absent.

2. **CY — Support in local y-direction**  
   - **Description:** Translational support stiffness in the structure’s local **y** direction.  
   - **Unit:** `kN/m²`  
   - **Default:** `0`  
   - **Interpretation:** A spring-like stiffness per area in the local y direction. If CY is zero, the model provides no y-direction support stiffness.

3. **CZ — Support in local z-direction**  
   - **Description:** Translational support stiffness in the structure’s local **z** direction.  
   - **Unit:** `kN/m²`  
   - **Default:** `0`  
   - **Interpretation:** A spring-like stiffness per area in the local z direction.

### Context and special handling note (torsional support vs. flange flexural stiffness)

The accompanying context states: **for the torsional support, the user has to manually add the flexural stiffness of the flange to the value DX**. This is specifically required **for the case where the support is created by the support CX or CY**. In other words, when the torsional behavior is influenced through supports defined by CX/CY, DX must be adjusted by including flange flexural stiffness in addition to the torsional stiffness value DX.  

Finally, these values (DX, CY, CZ) are **“active only for the subsequent MEMB input”**, meaning they should be set immediately before the MEMB step that consumes them, and not relied upon for later steps unless re-entered.

### Table description (MEMB / Design-element member definition and buckling context)

This table documents the input fields used by **BDK** for the **MEMB** (member) records, which define the structural member(s) to be analysed—typically for stability and buckling checks. The table is organized as “Item” entries, each with a **Description**, **Unit**, and **Default** value. It also clarifies how different numbering and reference concepts are used to select the correct structural entities.

#### Key concepts and reference model
- The **REF** item specifies the *reference type* that determines what the subsequent range/selection refers to. The table lists multiple possible reference types:
  - **BEAM**: a beam number
  - **SLN**: a structural line number
  - **TRUS**: a truss number
  - **CONT**: continuation record reference
- The table states default behavior: if no design-element identification is explicitly provided, **BDK** will try to use an **SLN number as the ID**. Additionally, when a sequence of structural lines is entered without a defined sequence ID, **BDK** may randomly choose an available ID.

#### Range/selection parameters
The table includes:
- **FROM**: first element number or structural line number (default **1**)
- **TO**: last element number (default is **TO = FROM** if not specified)
- **INC**: increment between element numbers (default **1**)
These fields enable defining a contiguous or patterned selection of elements for analysis.

#### Buckling-length modifiers
Two factor parameters define effective buckling lengths:
- **SKY**: effective buckling length factor for **major-axis bending**
- **SKZ**: effective buckling length factor for **transverse-axis bending**
Both are unitless and default to “not set” (shown as “-”), meaning the software will apply its internal/default buckling length handling unless overridden.

#### Member type selection
The **TYPE** field controls what mechanical behaviour the MEMB record represents. The table lists:
- **FLEX**: centric compression (flexural check context)
- **LAT**: major axis bending (lateral bending context)
- **LTB**: combined bending and axial compression
- **EIGE**: eigenvalues (eigenvalue-based buckling/eigen analysis)
Default **TYPE** is **LAT**. (The accompanying text emphasizes that for eigenvalue/buckling design, BDK may internally perform further eigenvalue analyses depending on the chosen standard, independent of how MEMB is specified.)

#### Design-element identification
- **ID**: identifies the **Design Element** number (used when design elements were created via **DECREATOR** and then called in **BDK** via **MEMB ID**).
The table shows the default as **SLN No.**, linking back to the described behaviour of ID assignment.

#### Input-order and continuation rule (from context)
MEMB records “conclude” the input definition: each **MEMB** must come **last** in the input order for the selected member, because it triggers the analysis definition completion. The **CONT** option allows defining a member spanning multiple structural lines (e.g., MEMB on SLN 5 followed by CONT entries for additional SLNs), enabling a combined member domain without inserting supports/bends/point loads between its ends so that a continuous deflection curve can be generated.

The input table is a structured report of **buckling eigenvalues and derived design resistance checks** for steel compression members, organized by analysis type and loadcase. It is intended to provide both **elastic buckling parameters** (critical forces/moments and slenderness) and **design-level resistances** (reduction factors applied per standard buckling curves), followed by **utilization ratios** that indicate adequacy.

## Main header / classification fields
- **BUCKLING EIGENVALUES**  
- **TYPE**: describes the eigenvalue analysis type (e.g., flexural, lateral, lateral torsional buckling), with fields such as **Type of eigenvalue analysis**.
- **No. Eigenvalue number**: identifies the eigenmode/order.
- **Buckling factor** and **Buckling factor EIGE/EIGE NO/ECHO**: includes numerical eigen-buckling factors and printing controls (flags like “ECHO”, “NO”).
- **Loadcase / Loadcase number**: maps results to a specific load scenario.
- **N-Ed [kN]**: design axial load (compressive force; noted as ≤ 0.0).
- **Maximum compressive force / Maximum moment**: the table references maxima of internal forces and moments used in the buckling assessment.

## Flexural buckling inputs (and elastic-to-design mapping)
- **M-y,Ed [kNm] / M-z,Ed [kNm]**: absolute maximum bending moments about the y and z axes.
- **My / Mz absolute maximum moment**: clarifies which values are used for resistance.
- **N-cr [kN]**: elastic critical flexural buckling force.
- **L-cr [m]**: comparative buckling length (effective length used in slenderness).
- **y–y, z–z comparative length**: indicates the buckling axis/effective length direction.
- **Buckling curve α**: buckling curve selection for cross-section classification.
- **Imperfection factor λ** and **non-dimensional slenderness χ**: slenderness-related parameters used to compute design reduction.
- **Reduction factor for flexural buckling**: used with **N-b,Rd [kN]**, the **design buckling resistance** for the compression member.

## Lateral buckling (LTB) section
This part extends the buckling assessment to **lateral torsional effects**:
- **M-cr [kNm]**: elastic critical lateral torsional buckling moment.
- **C-1**: moment factor depending on the bending moment diagram and support conditions.
- **LT recommended lateral torsional buckling curve α-LT**.
- **Imperfection factor for lateral torsional buckling λ-LT**.
- **Slenderness for lateral torsional buckling λ-LT** and related parameters:
  - **λ-LT0** (plateau length for the lateral torsional buckling curve)
  - **β** (value to determine reduction factor)
  - **χ-LT** reduction factor for LTB
  - **k-c** correction factor for moment distribution
  - **f** modification factor
  - **χ-LT,mod** modified reduction factor
- **M-b,Rd [kNm]**: design lateral torsional buckling resistance moment.

## Interaction factors (combined bending/compression)
- **INTERACTION FACTORS**
  - **k-yy, k-yz, k-zy, k-zz**: factors enabling interaction between axial load and bending components and/or between bending about orthogonal axes.

## Auxiliary terms for torsional effects
- **λ-0**: buckling due to uniform bending.
- **N-cr,T [kN]**: elastic critical torsional buckling force.
- **C-my,0, C-mz,0**: equivalent uniform moment factors.
- **Non-dimensional slenderness** (for lateral torsional): used for combined checks.

## Checks and utilization ratios
The table includes explicit **verification checks** by forming utilization ratios (often described as “buckling resistance according to EN 1993-1-1, Eq. 6.61/6.62”):
- **CHECK OF FLEXURAL BUCKLING / TORSIONAL BUCKLING**
  - **n-y = N-Ed / N-b,y,Rd**
  - **n-z = N-Ed / N-b,z,Rd**
- **CHECK OF LATERAL BUCKLING**
  - **m-y = M-y,Ed / M-b,Rd**
- **CHECK OF LATERAL TORSIONAL BUCKLING**
  - **m-z = M-z,Ed / M-b,Rd**
  - **n-y, n-z** repeated as needed
  - **nm-y, nm-z**: final buckling resistance expressions according to EN 1993-1-1 equations (i.e., interaction-formulated measures).

## Output control notes
The bottom part describes printing behavior depending on **selection type** (e.g., FULL vs NO/YES, and FLOW/FLEX/LAT/LTB). It indicates that either:
- **Only design values and corresponding utilization tables** are printed, or
- **All tables are printed**, or
- **Table is not printed** depending on flags.

Overall, the table is a comprehensive buckling eigenvalue-to-design workflow: it starts with **loadcase + elastic eigen results**, computes **slenderness/imperfection-dependent reduction**, produces **design resistances** for flexural and lateral torsional buckling, and concludes with **EN-formulated utilization ratios** using interaction factors.
